events.title: Google Chrome beta released
events.summary: Google launched Chrome in beta on September 2, 2008 — a minimalist browser built on WebKit with a multi-process architecture and the new V8 JavaScript engine.
events.about: Chrome treated each tab as a separate process for stability, shipped a blazing-fast JS VM (V8), and popularized the omnibox address bar. It quickly overtook Firefox and IE, drove the shift to evergreen auto-updates, and later forked WebKit into Blink — defining how modern browsers are built.

narrative.whyChosen: Chrome reset performance expectations and became the world's most-used browser.
narrative.whyImportant: V8, multi-process tabs, and rapid releases became the template every competitor followed.
narrative.problemSolved: Web apps like Gmail and Maps were pushing browsers to their limits; Google needed a platform built for applications, not just documents.

events.title: Lehman Brothers bankruptcy triggers global financial crisis
events.summary: Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 — the largest failure in U.S. history and the shock that froze credit markets worldwide.
events.about: Venture funding dried up, ad budgets collapsed, and enterprise IT projects were cut. Startups that had raised in 2007 suddenly faced down rounds or shutdowns; survivors like Airbnb and Uber later credited the crisis with forcing leaner product focus. Cloud adoption accelerated as CFOs demanded opex over capex — a tailwind for AWS and SaaS.

narrative.whyChosen: Lehman Monday is the date developers cite when startup funding and enterprise sales froze overnight.
narrative.whyImportant: The crisis reshaped startup survival strategies and accelerated the shift to cloud opex models.
narrative.problemSolved: This was a macro shock, not a product fix — it exposed over-leveraged finance and interconnected counterparty risk.

events.title: Stack Overflow public beta launches
events.summary: Joel Spolsky and Jeff Atwood opened Stack Overflow to the public on September 15, 2008 — a Q&A site with voting, accepted answers, and reputation for programmers.
events.about: Stack Overflow replaced forum chaos with one canonical answer per question — copy-paste from Google became 'stackoverflow.com/questions/...' in every codebase. Reputation, badges, and moderation scaled to millions of devs; the Stack Exchange network cloned the model for sysadmins, UX, and math. It shaped how programmers learn APIs and debug errors.

narrative.whyChosen: Stack Overflow became the default second brain for working programmers.
narrative.whyImportant: Voting and accepted answers made technical Q&A searchable and trustworthy at scale.
narrative.problemSolved: Forum threads buried good answers under noise and duplicate questions.
